title: Breadth-First Search
summary: Explore level by level with a queue to find shortest paths in grids and to simulate things that spread over time.
intro: Depth-first search dives down one path at a time. Breadth-first search fans out evenly with a queue, one step at a time, so it finds the shortest path and can model anything that spreads minute by minute.

steps.title: Queues in JavaScript
steps.body:
A queue is first in, first out: items leave in the order they arrived, like a line at a counter. JavaScript has no queue type, so you build one from an array.

The obvious version uses `push` to add and `shift()` to remove. It works, but `shift()` has to move every remaining element down one slot, so each removal costs O(n). Node hides this cost for small arrays, but on a queue of tens of thousands of items a search that should take milliseconds can take seconds.

The fast version never removes anything. Keep a `head` index that points at the next item to read:

```javascript
const queue = ["ada", "bo"];
let head = 0;
const first = queue[head++];
console.log(first, head); // ada 1
queue.push("cy"); // joins the back
```

`queue[head++]` reads the item at `head`, then moves `head` forward. The queue still has items while `head < queue.length`, so that is your loop condition. Items behind `head` stay in the array. That costs a little memory but makes every step O(1), constant time no matter how long the queue gets.

To send an unfinished item to the back of the line, `push` it again.

example.title: Print queue
example.prompt: Read print jobs as `name pages`, print at most 5 pages per turn from a head-index queue, and send unfinished jobs to the back.
example.output:
ada prints 5 (2 left)
bo prints 3 (0 left)
cy prints 5 (7 left)
ada prints 2 (0 left)
cy prints 5 (2 left)
cy prints 2 (0 left)
done after 6 turns
example.explanation: `runPrinter` copies the jobs into `queue` and reads them with `queue[head++]`. Each turn prints up to `perTurn` pages with `Math.min`. A job with pages left is pushed again, so it waits behind everyone already in line. The loop stops when `head` catches up with `queue.length`, and `turns` counts how many times a job was read.

practice.title: Coffee line
practice.prompt:
Read customers as `name visits` and print the order they are served in when each turn serves one visit.

1. Complete `serveOrder(customers)` using a queue with a `head` index (no `shift()`).
2. Each turn, read the next customer, push their name onto `order`, and subtract one from `visits`.
3. If the customer still needs visits, push them to the back of the queue.
4. Return `order`. The program prints it joined with `, `.

Input:

```text
ana 2
ben 1
cal 3
```

Expected output:

```text
ana, ben, cal, ana, cal, cal
```

tests.output: ana, ben, cal, ana, cal, cal
max, ivy, leo, kim, ivy, kim

hints: Copy the customers with `[...customers]` and start with `let head = 0`.
Loop with `while (head < queue.length)` and read with `const customer = queue[head++]`.
After `customer.visits--`, push the customer again only if `customer.visits > 0`.

steps.title: Shortest path in a grid

example.title: Maze exit
example.prompt: Read a maze of `.` and `#` with one `S` and one `E` and print the length of the shortest path, or -1 when E cannot be reached.
example.explanation: The queue starts with `[startRow, startCol, 0]`, and S is marked visited right away. Each dequeued cell checks for E, then pushes every open, unvisited neighbor with `dist + 1`, marking it visited as it goes in. Cells leave the queue in order of distance, so the first time E comes out its `dist` is the shortest path. If the loop ends without finding E, the function returns -1.

practice.title: From A to B
practice.prompt:
Read a maze with `A` and `B` and print the fewest steps from A to B, or -1 when B cannot be reached.

1. Complete `fewestSteps(grid)`. Use `findCell(grid, "A")` to get the start.
2. BFS with `[row, col, dist]` items in a head-index queue, moving up, down, left, and right through any cell that is not `#`.
3. Mark each cell visited in a boolean grid when you enqueue it.
4. Return `dist` when you dequeue `B`, or -1 if the queue runs out.

Input:

```text
A.#...
.##.#.
...#..
#.....
.#.#.B
```

Expected output:

```text
Fewest steps: 9
```
hints: Build `visited` with `Array.from({ length: rows }, () => new Array(cols).fill(false))`.
Start with `const queue = [[startRow, startCol, 0]]` and mark the start visited before the loop.
Skip a neighbor that is out of bounds, already visited, or `#`. Otherwise mark it and push `[nr, nc, dist + 1]`.

steps.title: Level by level and multi-source BFS

example.title: Spreading fire
example.prompt: Read a grid where fire spreads each minute from every `F` to neighboring `.` cells, and print how many minutes it spreads and how many floor cells never burn.
example.explanation: Every `F` goes into the queue before the loop, so both fires spread at the same time. Each pass of the `while` loop handles exactly `size` cells, one minute of spreading, and turns their `.` neighbors into `F`, which also marks them visited. `minutes` grows only when that round queued new cells. Afterwards, `grid.flat()` lists every cell and the `.` cells left over are the ones walls sealed off.

practice.title: Rotting oranges
practice.prompt:
Read a grid of oranges as rows of digits (0 empty, 1 fresh, 2 rotten) and print the minutes until every fresh orange rots, or -1 if some never do.

1. Complete `rotMinutes(grid)`. Push every rotten orange into a head-index queue before the loop.
2. Process one level per minute with `const size = queue.length - head`. A rotten orange rots its fresh neighbors up, down, left, and right: set them to 2 and push them.
3. Count a minute only when a round rotted at least one orange.
4. Return -1 if any 1 is left in the grid, otherwise the minutes. The program prints the result.

Input:

```text
211
110
011
```

Expected output:

```text
4
```
hints: The structure matches `spreadFire`: swap `"F"` for 2 and `"."` for 1.
After each round, `if (head < queue.length) { minutes++; }` counts only rounds that rotted something.
`grid.flat().includes(1)` tells you whether a fresh orange survived.

recap:
- A queue is first in, first out. Build it with `push` plus a `head` index and read with `queue[head++]`.
- `shift()` is O(n) because it moves every remaining element, so avoid it for big queues.
- `while (head < queue.length)` runs until the queue is empty.
- BFS reaches cells in order of distance, so the first time it reaches the target is a shortest path. Return -1 if it never does.
- Store `[row, col, dist]` in the queue and mark cells visited when you enqueue them, in a boolean grid or the grid itself.
- `const size = queue.length - head` processes one level per round, which is how you count minutes.
- Multi-source BFS pushes every source before the loop. Scan the grid afterwards to count cells it never reached.
